CO1: Run input and output scripts on a stack by hand and with a standard-library interpreter - pay to public key hash, the truth rule and separate execution - and say why Script is stateless and not Turing complete
CO2: Build and check scripted multisignatures and pay to script hash outputs: compute a redeem script, its hash and its address, count the signature checks and the bytes, and explain the dummy element and the limits on keys
CO3: Decide when an output with a lock time, OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY, a relative sequence, OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY or a flow-control script can first be spent, and which path of a multi-path script a given input script selects
CO4: Analyse how segregated witness changes authorization - witness programs, P2WPKH and P2WSH, bech32 addresses, nested forms, the BIP143 signature hash - and why it can be deployed as a soft fork
CO5: Analyse taproot and tapscript: the key tweak and the script tree, key path against script path, the control block, OP_CHECKSIGADD and the OP_SUCCESS opcodes, and what each spend reveals on the chain
CO6: Check the chapter's figures and statements against the BIPs, Bitcoin Core's sources and tests and real chain data, and say where each differs and what the difference changes

_note: These chapter objectives serve the course outcome LO-6 - to read and construct Bitcoin transactions, inputs and outputs, output and input scripts, authorization and authentication, signatures and fees, and to explain how a node decides whether a transaction is valid. CO1 to CO5 are its authorization half: running a script, building multisignature and script hash outputs, timelocks and flow control, segregated witness, and taproot. CO2 and CO5 serve LO-5 as well, because multisignature, output scripts and the scriptless multisignature are among the wallet designs that outcome compares. CO6 serves LO-3 as well, because its checks run a script interpreter against Bitcoin Core's own test data and read Core's sources at the pinned commit in place of a running node, which is not available in this environment. The signatures themselves, ECDSA and Schnorr, are developed in the next chapter.
